title: “Days and Nights in the Forest” Emerges from the Shadows
author: @NewYorker
content:
Four city jerks, privileged and frustrated young men from Kolkata, head to the countryside for a few days of slothful rest and rowdy dissipation. They approach the locals arrogantly, seeing the region’s poverty as a source for cheap, subservient help and an open field for heedless riot, but a series of chance encounters—and romantic entanglements—sends them home shaken and humbled, though maybe not wiser. This is the premise of Satyajit Ray’s 1970 melodrama “Days and Nights in the Forest,” which had long been hard to see until the release, earlier this year, of a 4K restoration, which has now arrived on the Criterion Channel. (It will also be released by the Criterion Collection, on Blu-ray and DVD, on September 29th.) The film is a teeming, turbulent, confrontational meld of emotion and observation, placing the eruptive pressure of societal conflict amid the seeming trivia of social life.

“Days and Nights in the Forest” is based on an autobiographical novel by Sunil Gangopadhyay, published in 1968. The feature’s literary basis is underlined when two of the men reminisce about a literary journal they founded long ago, but it’s palpable throughout, in the freewheeling actions and impulsive dialogue, which Ray nonetheless films with analytical detachment and gimlet scrutiny—as befits a work of personal experience that, however, isn’t his own but the author’s. (Ray’s critical distance from the characters is as crucial to the movie’s emotional power as is his wide-ranging empathy.) The movie’s anecdotal aspect both abstracts and expands the drama. Ray’s incremental approach to the story elides through lines and plot mechanisms in such a way that the crisscrossing relationships and events form an intellectual map of the forces underlying them.

From the start, there’s something dubiously bookish—callow and potentially callous—about the four men’s rustic jaunt. As Ashim (Soumitra Chatterjee), who planned the excursion, drives, Sanjoy (Subhendu Chatterjee) reads to the others from the back seat about Palamu, the region where they’re headed. The book he’s reading from leeringly describes the locale’s women as dark-skinned and scantily clad; the four men’s minds are on sex and love. They tease Hari (Samit Bhanja), also in the back seat, about a girlfriend leaving him; he pridefully asserts that he “dumped” her, but a flashback shows what really happened. Sanjoy is similarly teased about his relationship with his boss’s daughter, another source of resentment that shows up in a flashback. Meanwhile, the hyperactive, sardonic Shekhar (Rabi Ghosh), riding shotgun, is unemployed and claims to have no time for the “bourgeois” frivolity of romance.

The melodramatic force of Ray’s film is built into these spare but potent character sketches. Douglas Sirk, Hollywood’s supreme director of melodramas and a theoretician of the genre, spoke of his films’ dependence on the contrast between “immovable” characters and “split” ones. In “Days and Nights in the Forest,” Hari and Sanjoy, in the back seat, are the “split” characters, their flashbacks revealing the division between their present-tense façades and their bitterly remembered realities. Sitting up front, Ashim, who is coolly brazen, and the antic, unreflective Shekhar—the king and the jester—are the “immovable” ones, with unified identities that are nonetheless exposed and vulnerable.

All four are manifestly bourgeois, flashing their cash from the moment they arrive at the village where they are to stay. They blusteringly order a bedraggled local man named Lakha to accompany and serve them. (“Ask if he can come with us,” Sanjoy says to Ashim in English, certain that Lakha won’t understand.) They arrive as self-aware screwups, who know full well that they should have reserved their bungalow in advance but instead hector and bribe the guesthouse’s beleaguered watchman into bending the rules and giving them one anyway. He fears he’ll be fired for it, and one of the travellers—again in English—quips, “Thank God for corruption.”

The men are keen to go slumming. At night, they go drinking at a shedlike bar where women, to their surprise, drink together as heavily as men do. One of the women, Duli (Simi Garewal), noticing the haughty and higher-class men sizing her and her friends up, boldly approaches them for drinking money. The next morning, when the men show up at the local market in search of breakfast, a group of women, including Duli, are there in search of day labor. The men hire three, including Duli, to do their chores. One woman is pressed into service as a punkah wallah, charged with pulling a rope that keeps a hinged ceiling fan flapping back and forth and keeping the men cool. As for Duli, she sweeps the bungalow’s floor with a whisk broom, Hari ogling her as she bends over.

But Hari’s friends have other pursuits in mind. Shekhar brazenly asks Lakha where they can find “middle-class women,” and the poor man obediently points the way. As the four men walk the designated road, they pass a badminton court, where they encounter two women of the local gentry: Rini (Sharmila Tagore), a young, unmarried woman of intellectual ambition and poetic refinement, and her sister-in-law, Jaya (Kaberi Bose), a still youthful widow who is desperately lonely and the mother of a lively young boy. Surprised to encounter urbane menfolk here, the women lead them in a whirl of home visits—Rini’s father, Sadashiv (Pahari Sanyal), is a landowner—and social outings. Gradually, the women’s strong and probing personalities lay bare the weaknesses and presumptions of the ostensibly suitable men in their midst.

The men and women are instantly on familiar terms, and the push and pull of formalities and witticisms creates an atmosphere of brightness and romantic energy, although the household is darkened by tragedy and muffled by isolation. Rini guides Ashim to a small aerie that’s her solitary retreat, with her English-language books and her Western records (including “Rubber Soul” and “Joan Baez in Concert”), but their romantic connection is shadowed by her keen awareness of his cavalier, solipsistic arrogance. Jaya, with little hope of romance, seeks a sexual encounter, in a powerfully ironic scene contrasting the purity of desire with the fretful inhibitions of conventional morality.

As the story unfolds, relationships between friends, transactions with locals and bureaucrats, episodes of love and lust, and moments of painful self-awareness produce a subjective panorama of unredressed inequality, squandered energy, stifling tradition, and a restive quest for liberation. Ray gives his four men a natural exuberance and supplies them with a varied, pugnaciously expansive range of action. Whether in straightforward mealtime banalities or chatter when bathing at an outdoor well, or in the raucous ribaldry of their drunken rambles, they bring high spirits and a hunger for experience, albeit on their own presumptuous terms. Ray approaches the action with a vigorous yet reflective and piercingly probing eye. Observing the four men at the bar, his camera tracks from face to face, pausing at each before passing on, making palpable both connections and disconnections—isolation amid the overheated tumult.

The movie’s romantic centerpiece is a party game that the two women teach the four men during a picnic. It’s a memory game, in which the group sits in a circle, one member says the name of a famous person, and the next one repeats that name and adds another, and so on; those who forget a name are out, until a winner remains. For many movie lovers seeing the film for the first time, the game will be startlingly familiar, as it was more recently played in Wes Anderson’s “Asteroid City,” by a group of scientifically precocious teen-agers. (For that matter, the setup of Ray’s film also prefigures that of Anderson’s “The Darjeeling Limited.”) For both Ray and Anderson—who was involved in the current restoration and is a long-standing admirer of Ray’s—the demanding game gives rise to high drama and keen suspense along with tender comedy and rapturous romanticism. Both directors make use of its patterned and repetitive format to embody emotional extremes in a precise and formalized array of visual imagination.

The trivial outcome of this friendly competition plays an outsized role in the relationship of Rini and Ashim—a psychological wrangle in which the discerning Rini has the upper hand and lets him know it. (Ray films their climactic confrontation in intense, dual closeups, framed starkly against the sky, that are as indiscreetly intimate as they are sculpturally grand.) There’s another struggle, between Hari and Duli, that’s altogether more troubling, because of the inherent inequality of the relationship—between an educated middle-class man and a desperately poor and unworldly woman of doubtless little schooling who is also in his employ. Ray pays close attention to the fine points of the abusive relationship—including the confusion of emotion and the bedrock of money—and he situates it at the violent edge of class conflict and stifled revolt.

“Days and Nights in the Forest” came near the midpoint of Ray’s career. By 1970, he’d made more than a dozen features since his Neo Realist-inspired début, “Pather Panchali,” from 1955 (the first entry in his Apu trilogy, completed in 1959), and his work ranged from the historicist formalism of “The Music Room” to the ferocious urban feminism of “The Big City” to the time-shifting political modernism of “The Hero” to the antic musical fantasy of “The Adventures of Goopy and Bagha.” (He made his final dramatic feature in 1991, at the age of sixty-nine, the year before his death.) With “Days and Nights in the Forest,” he varies tones and moods widely within one drama as if also turning inward, considering urban intellectuals’ distance from India at large, the differences of experience, background, and identity that make connections either a struggle or an exploitation. His four city dwellers head home with more than just wounds. They bear symbolic souvenirs, physical and verbal, that they, like viewers, ignore at their own moral risk. ♦

title: Your Smartwatch May Not be as Smart as You Think it is - Nautilus
content:
Smartwatches have soared in popularity in recent years, and now roughly 30-40 percent of American adults own one of them. More than serving as just a timepiece or a second screen for notifications, these watches promise to monitor a growing number of health metrics—from blood pressure to sweat loss. But how accurate are they really? 

Featured Video

Kinesiologists from the University of Michigan recently published a new framework to help users understand what, exactly, smartwatches are measuring. 

Read more: “The Pitfalls of AI Health Coaches”

If you take a peek under the hood of your average smartwatch, you’ll find a suite of sensors, including an accelerometer, a gyroscope, GPS, and a photoplethysmogram (or PPG, which uses light to detect blood volume). These sensors collect raw data (acceleration, angular velocity, location, and optical signal data), and the good news is, they’re pretty accurate. 

But this data is just the input to the smartwatch, what users (and would-be consumers) are most interested in are the outputs. According to the researchers, this is where things get fuzzy. That’s because the signal provided by the raw data gets filtered through a layer of proprietary algorithms that churn out metrics like heart rate, physical activity, sleep duration, etc. The more recent the model, the more exotic the metric (i.e., water loss during exercise). 

According to the team, the farther from the sensory data the outputs are, the less accurate they are. For example, metrics like heart rate, step count, and outdoor pace are much more reliable than metrics like calories burned, sleep stages, blood glucose, and hydration loss. These “metrics” are more like estimates. 

“People shouldn’t take these metrics at face value,” study author Adam Lepley said in a statement. “In many cases, these devices are better suited to tracking trends over time, rather than as precise laboratory measurements.”

And that’s an important point. While these more exotic metrics may not represent a one-to-one agreement with lab-grade measures, they’re still useful for tracking your own progress over time. (Of course, the algorithms that generate the metrics are proprietary so if you switch brands they’re not likely to match.) The researchers also stress that any higher level recommendations from your devices, like exercise recovery time, should be taken with a grain of salt. 

In other words, listen to your body. It might be smarter than your watch.

title: I Went to the White House Brawl and Watched the Manosphere Go Limp
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
I found it easy to resist the early dispatches from “UFC Freedom 250,” the Ultimate Fighting Championship event held in June on the White House South Lawn. But Jon Ronson is the sort of writer I can’t help following into battle. Fresh off a new book about masculinity, Ronson brings a delightfully skewed perspective to the fights and the days that surrounded them. The result is a portrait of a planned media spectacle that can’t quite make sense of itself. The best battle here may be Ronson’s tussle with his own photographer, 79-year-old Bruce Gilden, who is a bit of a hugger.

“I’m pretty certain you hugged Stephen Miller first,” I say. “I don’t see Stephen Miller as initiating a hug.”

“You may be right,” he says. “I don’t remember. Look, I do things maybe other people aren’t comfortable doing, but I felt comfortable and I trust my instincts.”

He acknowledges that “nobody is immune to misreading a situation” and that because of him we were all forced back indoors, but he blames Miller’s entourage for not checking with their boss on whether he minded being hugged.

More on fighters, in and out of the ring

title: Worm munch matters: the new acoustic ecology of the soil | Aeon Essays
content:
Earthworms do not have a discernible mouth, a means to make sound, or ears, and most spend their lives burrowing below ground, eating soil and decaying organic matter. However, their behaviours produce sounds, which can reveal a surprising amount about the subterranean world in which they live. I’ve recently found myself leaning over a box of soil in the basement of my university department, headphones clutched to my ears, revelling in the soft, Velcro-like scrapes of earthworms eating. It sounds like this:

I have always loved earthworms. As a child on my parents’ allotment, I delighted in finding them in the soil as potatoes were dug in, fascinated by their soft, alien form wiggling in my hand. Now, I amuse my friends by ducking down in crowds at music festivals to rescue distressed earthworms from being squashed by the mob of muddy boots.

Until recently, my scientific research focused on the rapid patter and chop of bat echolocation calls, monitoring how their populations were responding to largely human-driven environmental change. I didn’t consider that the same ecoacoustic approaches could be applied below ground, to understand how earthworms are affected by us surface-dwellers. Fortunately, others had. I finally had a way to connect my scientific research speciality with my ardour for earthworms in the soil.

Worm munch might seem like a curiosity, but it represents a much bigger change in how we understand nature. More than just the behaviour of single creatures, such sounds can also reveal the health of whole ecosystems – and the underground is emerging as a new acoustic frontier.

Sound itself is a wave, a travelling vibration. Vibrancy is a word often used to describe colour and life. A vibrant ecosystem, therefore, is one that hums with the sounds of life.

While reading this essay, you can listen to a 15-minute recording of various sounds of the underground, collected in Oxfordshire in 2024:

Monitoring nature’s sounds has a long history. The ancient Greeks wrote poems and plays about birdsong and, in medieval England, the sounds of local birds gave many places their names. Today, an expert ornithologist will stand in a forest and conduct a bird survey using nothing but their eyes and ears.

However, when bioacoustics researchers in the 20th century began to place microphones or hydrophones and recorders in the field for days, weeks or months – known as ‘passive acoustic monitoring’ – they discovered whole new natural soundscapes. This technique has been especially powerful in realms where humans cannot stay for long, or for species that emit infrasonic or ultrasonic sounds beyond human hearing range (20-20,000 Hz).

Underwater habitats, for example, are difficult for people to be immersed in for extended periods without specialist equipment and training (for obvious reasons). Thus, collecting data on animals like whales and dolphins, which can traverse vast oceanic distances, was historically done with sightings from land or boats. That changed with passive acoustic sensors.

Bats use the returning echoes of their ultrasonic calls to build a sonic map of their surroundings

In the 1950s during the Cold War, the US Navy developed its Sound Surveillance System (SOSUS), an underwater network of hydrophones with the purpose of tracking Soviet submarines in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, originally code-named ‘Project Jezebel’. Arrays of hydrophones were deployed on the seafloor, connected via cables to the shore where the acoustic data could be monitored. While an original premise of this system was upheld – that enemy submarines would be easily tracked by their low-frequency sound signatures – the assumption that there would be little other noise in the ocean was not true. Sailors operating the SOSUS detected many other unknown sounds, including one they attributed to the ‘Jezebel Monster’. It took some years and the detective work of marine bioacousticians for this to be identified as the 20 Hz call of fin whales. Many other mysterious sounds began to be discovered, including the ‘boing sound’ and the ‘lightsabre sound’, both of which were also eventually attributed to minke whales. Since many cetaceans use sound for day-to-day activities – ranging from the low-frequency songs of blue whales to the whistles and high-frequency echolocation clicks of bottlenose dolphins – hydrophone technology has enabled these animals to be more fully understood as they move through the ocean.

Passive acoustic technology was similarly illuminating in demystifying bats and revealing one of their incredibly sophisticated evolutionary adaptations. Nearly all bats are nocturnal, relatively small, fly fast, and vocalise at frequencies mainly outside of human hearing, all of which makes them effectively invisible to people, or has caused them to be associated with evil and hence feared. Unless you’re looking for bats, you’re unlikely to notice them (although admittedly this is not true of larger fruit bats, which are hard to miss in parts of the world where they can congregate in cities in large numbers).

In the 1930s, the American physicist George W Pierce developed a method for detecting ultrasound using piezoelectric crystals and a sonic amplifier to study the ultrasonic sounds of birds and crickets. When the Harvard undergraduate Donald Griffin – who was convinced that bats were using sound for navigation – brought a cage of bats to Pierce’s lab, they discovered a cacophony of ultrasonic sound. Further research by Griffin and others revealed the full complexity of bats’ use of ultrasound, showing they used the returning echoes of their ultrasonic calls to build a sonic map of their surroundings, orienting themselves during rapid flight. Griffin termed this ‘echolocation’ – and ever since then it has allowed us to better understand the sonic world of the bat, which before was hidden in plain sight.

Although bioacoustic sounds have now been studied for decades, it’s only relatively recently that scientists have begun to use soundscapes to gauge ecosystem health, with the establishment of the field of ‘ecoacoustics’ in 2014. Ecoacoustics incorporates parts of bioacoustics, but also draws on the ideas of ‘soundscape ecology’, which traces back to the 1960s. As well as ‘biophony’ (animal sounds), ecoacoustics also incorporates geophony (sounds made by wind, rain, waves) and anthropophony (sounds made by humans or human activities).

A core principle of ecoacoustics is that complexly noisy natural places are healthier natural places. This means that it’s not just the volume of noise, but the diversity of sound that indicates habitat health. The dawn chorus in an intact Bornean tropical forest is magical in its complexity, especially if you’re lucky to experience it mixed in with the whoops of a troop of gibbons swinging through overhead, as I was during a visit in 2019.

In contrast, cities are generally not ecologically healthy and, while they are incredibly noisy places, they are filled with the harsh, more monotonous sounds of car engines and other machines, and often little biotic sound. Soundscapes dominated by anthropogenic sounds have been linked to poor mental health in people, whereas the opposite has been found for natural sounds like birdsong or forest soundscapes.

Carson demonstrated that the lack of spring’s dawn chorus in the US was due to the accumulation of DDT

A biotically silent landscape is a sign of nature collapse, as exemplified in Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962):

Over increasingly large areas of the United States, spring now comes unheralded by the return of the birds, and the early mornings are strangely silent where once they were filled with the beauty of bird song.

Collating scientific research, Carson demonstrated that the lack of spring’s dawn chorus in the US was due to the accumulation of DDT, a synthetic pesticide. DDT caused the thinning of bird eggshells and thus reproductive failure. Without Carson publicising the alarm of a silent landscape, resulting in the eventual ban of DDT in the US, many bird species may have been lost.

While the ecoacoustics of forests or cities are relatively straightforward to monitor, the underground world is more difficult to access. Monitoring earthworms and other soil-based creatures presents a similar challenge to listening to whales in the deep ocean or bats in the dark sky: there’s only so much an ear to the ground can hear. Yet by inserting acoustic probes or burying hydrophones into the soil, it’s possible to hear the rustling cacophony of an ant’s nest, the clicks of beetle larvae communication, and the scrapes of earthworm engineering.

Before I began listening in earnest to the underground, I almost solely used passive acoustic sensors to record bat echolocation and social calls, gleaning information on which species were where, how they were using different habitats, and how human actions were impacting their populations. I grew comfortable in this ultrasonic world and could pick out bat calls almost instantly when listening to recordings (slowed down to bring them into our hearing range), looking at a spectrogram. Transferring these skills to the low, soft sounds in the soil has been somewhat of a sonic culture shock.

The first time I listened to a soil soundscape, it felt like taking my first steps into an alien world. I’d spent so many years focusing on identifying sounds above ground, and now I had a portal into this earthy realm and a whole new acoustic space. Much of our recordings contain periods of little noise or near silence, punctuated by the unpredictable shuffles of something moving or something eating. I began to feel like Jodie Foster’s character Dr Ellie Arroway in the film Contact (1997), spending hours listening, searching for signals to decode and link to a biotic source or anthropogenic activity. Instead of ticking off in my head what the sources of the sounds might be, I’m often perplexed, imagining what the faunal, or otherwise, origins of the scratches, sifts, drums and buzzes could be.

We found post-midnight peaks in acoustic activity when earthworms are most active in the soil, and higher diversity under rewilded grassland

Here are two examples, one of which sounds like a laser, and the other like something buzzing:

Soil is the foundation of many ecosystems above ground: the medium from which plants grow, and the basis of most food chains. However, it also comprises complex ecosystems itself, filled with a high diversity of fauna, from microscopic bacteria to carnivorous mammals, which impact soil structure, function and chemical composition. And we’re finding that a healthy soil is often a noisier one.

Early results from studies using passive acoustics to assess soil health in garden, forest and farmland ecosystems have proved promising. Researchers have found associations between forest recovery and ecoacoustic measurements of soil soundscapes, suggesting healthy soils do sound significantly different. In my own research, we are testing the use of passive acoustic monitoring for assessing soil health and the effectiveness of nature recovery approaches in UK grassland landscapes. Unlike previous soil ecoacoustic projects, we have collected continuous 24-hour recordings across our sites, which has revealed dynamic patterns in the soundscapes from day to night. We found post-midnight peaks in acoustic activity when earthworms are most active in the soil, and higher diversity under rewilded grassland, compared with intensively grazed cattle pasture. Concurrent to the ecoacoustic data, we conducted traditional soil biodiversity sampling, scooping up large and tiny soil-dwelling animals, such as earthworms, ants, woodlice, millipedes, beetles and insect larvae. Earthworms made up most of the soil invertebrates, and we believe their movements are contributing significantly to the soil soundscape.

Why? Earthworms are soil ecosystem engineers. Their burrows change the soil structure, and different types of earthworms have different burrowing behaviours – vertical or horizontal, deep or shallow – which allow air and water to flow. Earthworms also break down dead plant and animal matter into smaller pieces, which are fed on by bacteria and fungi, releasing nutrients that would otherwise be trapped. That’s why counting earthworms is a common method for assessing soil health in agricultural settings.

To meet internationally agreed goals for biodiversity restoration, we need systematic and standardised ways to monitor soil health. Traditional techniques require costly manual effort, followed by laboratory analysis for chemical indicators, such as pH and nutrient availability, or physical indicators, such as water-holding capacity, texture and compactness, or biological indicators, such as soil enzymes, microbial biomass and diversity, and soil carbon. The effort means such tests can be conducted only at relatively small scale, sampling only snapshots of the soil.

Passive acoustic sensors, by contrast, can be buried in the soil and left to collect data over multiple days, with multiple sensors buried simultaneously in different locations. A healthy soil where natural biological processes are intact will sound different to a depleted or chemically scarred soil due to the differences in diversity and abundance of animals living in it, the physical properties, and resulting structure. At least that’s the ecoacoustic theory.

Since underground ecoacoustics is a young field, we’re still ironing out details, discovering unknowns, and encountering challenges. Firstly, some ecoacoustic methods for analysing environmental soundscapes are based on the premise that audible biotic sounds are made between 2,000-15,000 Hz and anthropogenic sounds between 1,000-2,000 Hz. This was defined on the frequency range of bird calls, but it already causes headaches for researchers in areas with a lot of anthropogenic sounds, such as cities, where machines emit sounds across the frequency spectrum. The problem may be particularly acute in soil ecoacoustics, because much of the sounds we’re recording are between 1,000-3,000 Hz, spanning both the ecoacoustically defined biotic and anthropogenic categories.

A second thing we’re learning is that only a small fraction of soil organisms are acoustically detectable. Unlike bats or crickets or frogs or whales, earthworms and other soil organisms do not shout to find their way around, nor trill and whoop to attract mates. In fact, earthworms don’t make any deliberate sounds at all. Movement sounds alone are incredibly difficult to assign to specific species as they don’t have a function, like bat echolocation. However, if we can link some of these soil sounds to broad functional groups, this will give us better insight into soil health and above-ground habitat, enabling us to unpick what is driving differences between sites.

We are on the cusp of unearthing and understanding a subterranean soundscape never heard before

A third major challenge is the lack of available libraries on soil faunal sounds with which to verify signals in our recordings. However, we are starting to build these. While others are focusing on beetle sounds, such as those made by dung beetles under cow pats, we have started with the earthworms. By listening to earthworms in a bespoke soundproof worm habitat (a 0.5 m3 wooden box covered in soundproof foam and filled with soil), with no other fauna present, we can confirm we’re hearing the same worms in the field.

1 of 4

We also still need to unpick confounding factors that affect the soil soundscape. For instance, the impact of soil type and moisture on sound transmission is not well known, yet it will impact the sounds recorded. The dispersion of sound in the soil is complicated. Fortunately, there is a significant body of research outside ecoacoustics, focusing on detecting cracks in oil pipes and similar important, buried infrastructure, that has tackled this problem. So work is underway to translate this to our field.

Finally, there are the physical challenges. Soil type and moisture also affect the ability to actually get the acoustic sensors into the soil. In July 2025, a couple of students and I were conducting a small-scale soil ecoacoustic survey on a Cotswolds-based regenerative farm; temperatures were above 30°C and it hadn’t rained for weeks. The ground was rock solid, making digging the roughly 10 cm-deep holes for the hydrophones incredibly difficult. It took us bouncing on top of spades like pogo sticks to make any headway. We ran into a further extreme weather-related challenge with the effect of high heat on the recorder’s portable battery, which drained power quicker than anticipated.

However, all of this is part of the learning process with new field techniques. And the bigger picture? We are on the cusp of unearthing and understanding a subterranean soundscape never heard before.

Sound is a tangible way of connecting to aspects of nature that are hidden from humans. The deep ocean, the dark night, and now the dense earth beneath our feet. Listening to realms that may seem devoid of life invokes new understanding and can highlight the vibrancy of life, thriving in overlooked places.

What other uncanny sounds will we encounter in the subterranean realm, and what might they tell us about nature recovery? Like the oceanic hydrophone network, eventually we could have a Soil Sound Surveillance System (a SOSOSUS, if you will) buried in fields, woodlands, savannahs and moorlands, monitoring the hidden world beneath our feet. Maybe we’ll discover an underground ‘Jezebel Monster’.

‘What is it like to be a bat?’ was the question posed by the philosopher Thomas Nagel, in his essay about understanding the experiences of others and differences in perception. Bioacoustics opened up the world of bat echolocation and sonic sensory experience. Perhaps, through understanding sonic vibrations in the soil, we can unlock an experience even more alien than a bat’s, prompting the question: What is it like to be an earthworm?

This essay was developed within a partnership between the Leverhulme Centre for Nature Recovery and Aeon.

title: Kai Bird on Roy Cohn, a Founding Father of Donald Trump’s America
author: @NewYorker
content:
Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen

Sign up for our daily newsletter to get the best of The New Yorker in your inbox.

During the height of Roy Cohn’s friendship with Donald Trump, according to the historian Kai Bird, “they were on the phone with each other a dozen times a day.” Bird’s new book, “American Scoundrel,” details Cohn’s profound influence on Trump—whom he met as a young real-estate heir in the nineteen-seventies—and how Cohn is “haunting” politics in our time. “I had written about Roy Cohn in [previous biographies] as this nefarious, minor, awful figure who was disruptive and divisive and unethical. And I suddenly realized that the establishment that I’d been writing about for forty years is gone. Their values and culture, the politics, the bipartisanship . . . That’s all gone,” he tells David Remnick. “Roy Cohn explains something about the dark side of America that I just didn’t understand.” They discuss Cohn’s early career as a prosecutor and his role as the “mastermind” of the McCarthy purges; his service as a lawyer and fixer for Mafia members, politicians, and celebrities; and an allegation of being involved in sex trafficking.

Further reading and listening:

  • “How Roy Cohn Taught Donald Trump Everything,” by Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark
  • “The Mobster Cosplay of Donald Trump,” by David Remnick
  • “Adapting Oppenheimer’s Life Story to Film, with Biographer Kai Bird,” an episode of The New Yorker Radio Hour
  • “Roy Cohn and the Making of a Winner-Take-All America,” by Naomi Fry

title: The Principled Cynicism of “By Any Means”
author: @NewYorker
content:
In a way, the most important review of “By Any Means” is a synopsis, because the film, as a title card declares, is “based on true events,” and the events themselves are unspeakable and need to be widely known. The story is set mainly in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, in 1966, and is centered on the killing, that year, of a Black businessman and civil-rights activist, Vernon Dahmer, Sr. (played here by Giancarlo Esposito), who was targeted by the Ku Klux Klan because of his efforts to register Black voters. More generally, the movie, directed by Elegance Bratton, is about the historical context of this murder, the conscious and organized effort by white Southern citizens and officials to intimidate, persecute, and subjugate Black people. The action is rooted in that racist reign of terror—and the fear that it sowed. Thus, the film, both as a history lesson and as a flash point of current politics, takes on a great responsibility and a grave one.

The local F.B.I. office, in Jackson, Mississippi, begins to investigate the killing, but some locals are too afraid to tell what they know, others too full of hate, so the F.B.I. decides to make use of Gregory Scarpa, Sr. (Mark Wahlberg), a white mobster and hit man from Brooklyn who was serving as a government informant. (Scarpa’s involvement, though widely reported, hasn’t been officially acknowledged by the F.B.I.) In 1964, Gregory had helped the F.B.I. locate the bodies of three slain activists—James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Mickey Schwerner—and “By Any Means” opens with a view of the assistance he provided: he ties a white man to a chair and tortures him, beating him with a baseball bat.

Tasked with finding out who killed Vernon, Gregory is accompanied by a Black F.B.I. agent named Wayne Strider (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II), who’s assigned to work as his handler. (This character is a composite of various agents, whereas Scarpa, who died in 1994, is entirely real.) The film is dominated by the two men’s relationship. Wayne, a native of Hattiesburg who recently returned from a long posting in Chicago, has been frustrated that his boss at the F.B.I. office, a white man named Roy K. Moore (an actual historical personage, here played by David Strathairn), keeps him and the office’s two other Black agents from working on civil-rights-related cases. So he accepts this top-secret mission with at least a modicum of enthusiasm. Having been a friend of the murdered man, he’s especially motivated to gather information about the killers, but he’s dubious about Gregory’s methods, which he witnesses up close on the first day of their partnership.

Wayne picks Gregory up at a motel, in Mobile, Alabama, and hands him a briefcase containing, among other things, a gun. As the pair drive by night to Hattiesburg, they’re stopped on a lonely country road by a white police officer. When Wayne presents his F.B.I. badge, the officer, either incredulous or enraged, accuses him of impersonating a federal official, slams him onto the hood of the car, and is about to shoot him at point-blank range when Gregory guns down the cop; to make extra sure, he shoots him again on the ground. Wayne is aghast—he is, after all, an officer of the law. “You shot a cop,” he exclaims. “We’re fucked.” Gregory responds, “No, he’s fucked.” I won’t spoil the upshot; suffice it to say that Wayne had no idea what Gregory had been up to in the area in 1964 and that Gregory fills him in on the backstory.

The prime dramatic mechanism of “By Any Means” is Wayne’s conversion—first grudging, then fervent—to Gregory’s methods. To start with, knowing the lay of the land, he guides their investigation but hesitates to set foot in segregated spaces, such as a gun shop where a weapon used against Vernon was sold. And he vehemently refuses to take part in the violence that’s Gregory’s method. But the physical threats ramp up. Attacked by whites in the street and facing violence at the house where he lives with his wife, Allison (Nicole Beharie), Wayne makes common cause with Gregory. Although there’s a practical and personal basis to Wayne’s newfound commitment, there’s also a philosophical one that’s reflected in the movie’s title. Wayne is effectively caught between the nonviolence advocated by Martin Luther King, Jr. (whose book “Why We Can’t Wait” he keeps in his car) and the teaching of Malcolm X, who made “by any means necessary” an iconic phrase of the civil-rights movement in a 1964 speech. Gregory says that he likes Malcolm—and quotes that very phrase. Wayne says that he wants to “put those crackers in jail” and asks Gregory what he’d do with them if he were Black. “Kill them all, every last one,” the gangster answers. Neither Wayne nor, apparently, anyone else he knows in Hattiesburg has entertained any such plan; nonetheless, the expression of it, however flip, suggests a counterfactual political fantasy that would make “One Battle After Another” seem downright passive.

There’s a tendency all too common in crime dramas that I’m tempted to call convenient incompetence: a major crime is committed, but police, media, and even lay people fail to notice much about it, handily allowing the plot to proceed without the complex interference of things that would certainly occur in the real world. In a way, it feels churlish to pick at “By Any Means” for this, because, at its best moments, it honors the exalted struggles that it dramatizes. This is the director Bratton’s second feature; his first, “The Inspection,” from 2022, based loosely on his own experience as a Black and gay marine in the age of “don’t ask, don’t tell,” is rich in such spiritual energy even as it looks analytically at the institution of the military in American civic and domestic life. The best moments in “By Any Means” build on that achievement. When Wayne and his wife attend Vernon’s voter-registration rally and a subsequent gathering at his home, she tells Vernon and his wife, Ellie (LaChanze), of Wayne’s frequently repeated line that “America won’t be right until Mississippi is right.” And there’s a fine scene in which Gregory, assuming that Wayne is the first Black F.B.I. agent, calls him the agency’s Jackie Robinson; Wayne responds with the names of a number of early Black agents, including the one believed to be the first, James Wormley Jones, who joined in 1919.

The movie’s very premise, the F.B.I.’s extreme effort to find Vernon’s killers, is just one of several elements in the film that may produce a kind of agonizing nostalgia. Despite the manifest horrors it confronts, “By Any Means” depicts a functioning federal government that has passed civil-rights legislation, enforced it (yes, even by any means necessary), and doesn’t have to worry about bad-faith Supreme Court decisions negating or neutering it. There is a President, Lyndon B. Johnson, who has no intention of letting vigilantes and racist local law enforcement “make a mockery” of the civil-rights legislation that he’s got through Congress. Even the plain and factual reporting of news on the radio seems like a vanished trace of an ancient society.

Still, the movie does at times rely on convenient incompetence. When white people get beaten up or injured, as gravely as by torture or as dramatically as in a car chase, the police appear to be unaware or indifferent, as do Black and white townspeople alike. A dead white police officer sparks no apparent interest, outcry, or investigation. There’s a noteworthy scene, sickening but instructive, in which a local Klan leader speaks to a handful of fellow-marauders and lays out a litany of grievances against Black people rooted in historical myth, economic anxiety, and class resentment, railing at the prosperity of one Black man rather than at the wealth of many white grandees. But the Black community’s politics—for that matter, politics in any practical sense—is entirely elided.

Above all, the script, by Sascha Penn, doesn’t give Wayne much interiority and offers little chance for him to express himself. The action takes place in a vacuum, sealed off from inner lives as from wider currents. In place of a view of history, “By Any Means” puts forth a Machiavellian world view: as the face of policy, nonviolent protest and law-abiding law enforcement are best—but, in practice, governments and activists alike will only succeed through ruthless, albeit covert, violence.

That’s why the movie’s many powerful moments are undercut by occasional, discordant touches that bring to mind the misjudgments of “Green Book” (2018), in which, similarly, a slickly rugged Italian New Yorker travels by car with a Black man down South and schools him in the cruder side of life (which that awful movie portrays as the authentic Blackness that its Black protagonist is missing). There’s no such animus in “By Any Means,” but the changes in attitude toward the strategic use of violence that Wayne undergoes as a result of his relationship with Gregory, are something he doubtless reflects on. He’s warned by his superiors to keep the mission a secret. Does he nonetheless talk with his wife, or with a friend? If not, is the secrecy of his hard mission weighing on him? And who is the person on whom it would be weighing, the person behind the badge, behind his official responsibility and self-designated purpose? “By Any Means” is often stirring but often infuriating. In shaping it as an action movie, Bratton makes it a tale of types, not of lives led but of pieces on the chessboard of history. ♦

title: Taking In the Scene at Daisy Chain Fields, the Zoomer Lilith Fair
author: @NewYorker
content:
Olivia Rodrigo’s daylong, woman-led event felt at times like any other corporate music festival. But, if music is the measure, it was up to something stunning.

September 2, 2026

Photograph by Mario Anzuoni / Reuters

A music festival ostensibly unfurls itself for music fans, but the experience of one can give lovers cause for doubt. Its contemporary format impresses, firstly, as an altar to capital. Tickets are priced at tiers that smell extortionate, and are won by either facing off with bots or succumbing to the—actually extortionate—resale market. And the sell doesn’t end there, what with the soaring concession prices and the branded outposts that one must dodge before hearing a single note. God-wrought and man-made hazards abound: bad drunks and bad trippers, theft, brawling, crowd crush, sexual assault; heat and dust and rain and their hellish coagulation, mud. For the first time in a long time, this summer, I attended Lollapalooza, a four-day event during which the sky never fails in its offering, transforming, under booted and flip-flopping feet, the manicured lands of Grant Park into sludge. My waxer told me of a client who got her foot stuck among a moving throng—her leg went snap. People get hurt at music festivals; people die. In the least worst outcome, they have a bad time and swear off returning—but may give next year’s lineup a gander, you know, just ’cause. Because music compels in that way. Call it above nature.

Music is a hard business in any era. In this one, even as live events are promoted as “experiences,” set apart from the virtuality of streaming, ticket sales—once considered a reliable means for artists to make money off their songs—seem increasingly unpredictable. This year, the struggle found a diagnosis, “blue dot fever,” after the azure daubs denoting unsold seats on Ticketmaster, the largest ticketer of live events in the world. Festivals, with their many equity pipers to pay, contend with further caprices. Two weeks ago, one of the majors, Bonnaroo, held annually in Tennessee since 2002, announced that, despite extensive—and, likely, costly—construction to improve the locale’s “resiliency to Mother Nature,” and owing to years of intense summer storms, the festival would be “taking a much-needed year off in 2027.”

The event I attended in Irvine, California, this past Saturday, then, was a work of tremendous gall. Fourteen women-fronted acts, plus a few guests, performed, for free, a benefit show to raise money for charitable organizations aiding women and girls. Not a new idea, but not easily done—and it’s been a minute. The festival, Daisy Chain Fields, reflects the mettle of Olivia Rodrigo, the twenty-three-year-old pop star. Since her 2021 début, “Sour,” Rodrigo has become a likable ambassador for her generation, awing an elder commentariat with her taste—her favorite Weezer album is “Pinkerton”—and her capable approach to celebrity. She is unshy yet unshrill about her beliefs. Amid quibbles over what ethics can reasonably be expected from stars pushing art product, Rodrigo makes music about what it feels like for girls while championing their autonomy, and the latter does not sound like lip service. Her last tour raised money for abortion funds and brought in local groups to distribute reproductive-health resources on site, a charitable act met with praise and also censure from a state politician in Missouri who said that Rodrigo “should be ashamed” for “championing abortion.”

Rodrigo, who has also expressed empathy for Palestinians and has condemned ICE, says this is what artists do. It’s an old mantle, one that has the feel of skipping a certain, once conspicuous generation. The millennials who repackaged girl power have gone rather quiet at this hour, lending credence to the suspicion that all that “run the world” talk was not for “we” but “me.” The obvious and stated precursor to Daisy Chain Fields is the Gen X mainstay Lilith Fair, the touring festival of female artists sprung from Sarah McLachlan’s justified ire over sexism in the music industry. Its nineties iteration was a riotous success (the 2010 revival, less so), raising more than ten million dollars, across the decade’s last three summers, for women-focussed charities. The 2025 documentary “Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery” reintroduces its subject as lost knowledge left to be recovered by Zoomer women. Rodrigo appears in the film as the first talking head, telling the camera she is stunned that she had only learned of the festival a few years prior, and marvels that her favorites—McLachlan, Sheryl Crow, Pat Benatar, Fiona Apple, Jewel—had been there.

But Rodrigo is after something apart from a reboot. Righteous as McLachlan’s endeavor was, she asserted a firm hierarchy. “I think any social or political issues are secondary, although very important, because it is a music festival first and foremost,” she told CNN in 1998. Rodrigo has another relation in mind, something causal, catalytic. Daisy Chain Fields was “founded on the belief that joy, community, and creativity can inspire meaningful change,” she writes in the festival’s mission statement. “Beyond its philanthropic impact, Daisy Chain’s core purpose is to cultivate joy and shared understanding, creating space for meaningful moments of connection across generations and communities.”

Were philanthropy its sole end, the festival would have succeeded before it opened its doors. At a Friday press conference, Rodrigo, dressed in a pink minidress custom-made by the Palestinian brand Nöl Collective, announced that Daisy Chain Fields had already raised ten million dollars, to be shared among its ten nonprofit partners, each dedicated to the health, safety, and flourishing of women and girls: Baby2Baby, Black Mamas Matter Alliance, Center for Reproductive Rights, FreeFrom, Jhpiego, Johns Hopkins Center for Indigenous Health, National Domestic Workers Alliance, National Institute for Reproductive Health, National Women’s Law Center, and Planned Parenthood.

But there is that preposition from the mission statement, “beyond.” And another phrase, “meaningful change.” Rodrigo’s festival intends to raise consciousness alongside funds, alongside and as a consequence of the sound. But how to measure such a thing?

The question came to mind when I arrived at the festival grounds, in Irvine’s Great Park, at 11 A.M., in time for the first set, Quiet Light, the self-produced dream-pop artist and Texan who moonlights as a medical student. On time is late for getting barricade, a festival ritual that escaped my knowledge until fairly recently. You can find videos of this act, people camping for hours outside a festival’s gates, then rushing full bore across the grounds for a choice spot abutting the necessary barrier between fan and stage, then staying put until their favored headliner arrives. This is one way to enjoy a festival these days, and Daisy Chain Fields was no exception. Not for Crystal and Carley, a mother and daughter, who were seated on a blanket and sharing a handheld fan. As Coachella regulars, this was not their first rodeo. “What’s important for us is to get barricade today,” Carley, a recent college grad, who had jogged ahead in her Doc Martens to reserve a place for both of them, said.

Crystal, who is forty-seven, had been to Lilith Fair when she was her daughter’s age. “Sarah McLachlan, Sheryl Crow, Indigo Girls,” she recalled. “Only women. It was just amazing.” She and Carley were there for that spirit, for the causes—“helping women, and young girls especially, because in a lot of the United States we don’t have the autonomy to make decisions for our reproductive rights,” Carley said. They were barricading for Rodrigo and her set’s guests, Stevie Nicks and McLachlan, who would not take the stage for another eight hours. “Oh, my gosh, and Doechii” (on in about five).

Performances alternated between two stages—Marigold and Dandelion—without overlap, in theory giving all forty-five thousand attendees a shot at laying eyes and/or ears on every set. In practice, this worked for a time. Walking at a motivated but not harried pace, I could reach earshot of the opposite stage within six minutes or so—a number that climbed with the hours and arrival of more bodies, each with their own idea of traffic flow. For that is another way festival people spend their time, milling about in the manicured space between stages, seeing what else, aside from music, might be worth consuming. Brooks, the running-shoe company and a festival sponsor, gave away blankets to anyone who signed up for its Run Club, while Taco Bell served free Baja Blasts in the flavor “You Seem Pretty Pink for a Baja Blast,” punning on the title of Rodrigo’s recent studio album.

Per the ad-speak that seems to have leapt into everyone’s lexicon over the years, these are “activations” and a staple of the modern music festival. These moments of commerce at the festival were contiguous with its art installations, such as “Fata Morgana (Lost & Found),” by the Angeleno artist Kelly Wall, a functional penny press that rewards participants with the customary flattened souvenir, and Yoko Ono’s “Wish Tree,” another interactive piece that asks audiences to write their wishes on pieces of paper and tie them to tree branches—“one of the many thoughtful activations,” as a review of the festival published by The Cut put it.

Lines for products or experiences or the synergy of both stretched and wound through the grounds, commingling with other lines: lines for merch, lines for photo ops, lines for food, lines for a custom hot-pink Nalgene—with a twenty-dollar donation to REVERB, a nonprofit greening concerts and festivals—and lines to fill it for free. It was not always evident what anyone awaited. I was reminded of one of my favorite jokes from “South Park,” in which the boys queue for what feels like forever in an experience that turns out to be “the Line Ride, a real-life simulator of a long line.” The weather in Irvine—shy of a hundred degrees before noon, and humid—was punishing. As I left Quiet Light’s set, I walked past someone receiving medical assistance at the Lego Editions activation.

A festival is a joyful endurance test, as are marathons. People make do. By midafternoon, no shadowy patch was left vacant; shade became a valuable resource, even if it meant swaying to Mitski from afar. One of the bill’s two millennials, Mitski supplemented officially posted cooling tips with friendly reminders of her own. “If you feel faint, no shame, just sit down where you are. It’s fine, it’s fine. It’s better than falling,” she told the audience. “And, if you have sunscreen, please apply sunscreen. . . . If you don’t have sunscreen, forget about it. It’s fine, never mind, it’s too late.” It was around 4 P.M.

Staff distributed cold, wet towels for necks—another souvenir—and tossed boxed water into outstretched hands. When someone dropped, people parted for medics. Prone to a midday jog during a heat wave, I am aware of what augurs heatstroke, and became my own bellwether. Two women introduced me to a cooling technique they called “nipple ice.” They’ve had “something” every month this year—Zara and Florence and Qveen Herby and Thot Squad, Warped Tour—with more shows on the docket.

One of the women told me that her husband works “in production” and she imparted her brass-tacks read on the scene: “Something like this has a lot of grab because of the charity aspect and everything.” Her friend, holding the ice, added, “Not to mention the headliners.” Aside from a fallen vape, seized at security, they applauded the smoothness of the operation, a credit, said the first, to the festival’s producer, C3 Presents (also a subsidiary of Live Nation, which owns Bonnaroo). I spoke with someone else, in from L.A. with his daughter, who also sang the company’s praises. “C3 does a really good job.” I cannot lend nipple ice the same endorsement.

The people would not be deprived of their festival drag, thank God. Flower child was not the only theme, though there were crowns aplenty. I saw kaffiyehs and cowboy boots—tan and shiny pink—dolphin shorts with “CUNT” on the butt, mesh shirts, jerseys, Sambas, Chucks, a “Protect the Dolls” tee, a “Girls Invented Punk Rock” crop top, a shirt airbrushed with “MAGGOTS FOR BRAINS” (track No. 4 on Rodrigo’s latest album). There were baseball caps representing My Chemical Romance; the Avett Brothers; “FUCK ICE”; the Oilers; HBO’s “I Love LA”; Shellback Tavern, located in Manhattan Beach, California; and many, many, many camo Midwest Princesses. The crowd leaned young and femme, though unaccompanied grown folks put up a good showing. (If there was an implicit rhyme to the distribution of the lineup, Marigold—with the Breeders and Garbage on deck—entreated an older, or at least punkier crowd; no performer between three and 7 P.M. was younger than fifty-five.) Various parent-child pairings intrigued me, how they were held fast, it seemed, by something radder than supervision.

Shall I be a vibe kill and ask about politics? The sometimes bummer of Daisy Chain Fields was a product of its resemblance to other corporate festivals, and, when it was a drag, it was a drag in the way that other corporate festivals can be a drag—perhaps impeding its mission of change through joy. The wait for an educational exhibition called Daisy Chain Reaction was, by noon, an hour and counting. “And by the time I got in . . . I did not have enough time to stay in there,” one woman told me outside the building where the exhibition was housed. At thirty-seven, she missed out on Lilith Fair, she told me, but felt that now was the time—for Bikini Kill, Chappell, and Rodrigo. A member of the D.S.A. and active in her workplace’s union, she would not overstate the liberation of the occasion. “This is definitely a capitalist event, right?” she said. “Even though all the proceeds are going to these organizations, we still have these weird brand activations. But you have to balance things, I guess, at this point in time.” Most everyone else I spoke with voiced their support for women’s rights in the usual liberal idiom, gesturing vaguely toward the state of things. (Though perhaps some vagueness is due to a person talking politics in a hundred-degree heat.)

Music quells what it will. Joyful noise and other, impolite sounds radiated from the sets oscillating between the two sites. Cut the platitudes, this was it: we were here for Die Spitz and Santigold, for Rachel Chinouriri and Bikini Kill. If music is the measure, Daisy Chain Fields was up to something stunning. The artists seemed to have a sense of themselves as pedagogues, leaving lessons in how to work your shit. Certain images stick with the sounds: Kathleen Hanna, of Bikini Kill, flinging her form around; Doechii, fat-assed and painted fuchsia; Star Amerasu, in her Pink Pony getup, m.c.’ing at the behest of Chappell Roan. Every vocalist, it seemed, had a twirl, a scream. The sign-off from Die Spitz was a shout from Eleanor Livingston, “Free Palestine! Fuck ICE!” From the stage, “girls” was returned to the capacious identity it ever was—for gays, for theys, for the dolls, wherever they were. Even Rodrigo, the almost too-good student who should make a mess someday, went total sprite, toying with everyone’s jugular. She genuflected, then dueted with those whom without her art would not exist: Sarah McLachlan (who gave tribute, in turn, to the late Dolly Parton), a surprise Alanis Morrisette, and Stevie Nicks, who we craved and dreaded hearing sing about “gettin’ older, too.” A show, folks. Rodrigo has already intimated a repeat.

The festival was an impressive feat of planning and production, an execution of vision that may or may not translate into alternative, insurgent thought or actions. Playing the cynic, I could select any number of cynical examples that suggest not. Not since a surprise appearance by Kanye West at the White Sox stadium years and years ago have I seen the sort of mad rush toward Katseye, the turbulent girl group whose remaining members were unable to perform as planned that day, but briefly went onstage to introduce representatives from the organization Baby2Baby, which provides basic necessities to children in need—a rush followed just as quickly by an exodus when the group left our sight. But cash is king, as they say. “Just by being here you are shedding light on these issues,” a representative from the Center for Reproductive Rights, who took the stage just before the Breeders came out, told us. No use sniffing at ten million dollars of charity in this world. By the end of the night, that figure, Rodrigo announced, had doubled, this time thanks to a matching gift from a professional philanthropist, Melinda French Gates. No good sniffing at any of that, either. What’s the harm in feeling good, anyway? When’s the last time we had a feel-good about feeling good? And what happened next? ♦

title: What Happens When a Kid’s Robot Best Friend Dies?
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
In this story for MIT Technology Review, Sara Harrison explores the field of social robotics and the growing use of robot companions as therapy for autistic and other neurodivergent kids. These playful machines show promise: Research suggests that they can help children practice social skills and offer something overworked therapists and exhausted parents can’t—a patient companion, available 24/7. But Harrison also reports on their limitations and risks. Does this approach truly work? What about all the data gathered on the child? And what happens when a robot friend suddenly stops working and “dies”? A fascinating and unsettling look at tech that has moved into the most intimate corners of a family’s home.

While Moxie found herself in more and more people’s homes, Embodied still struggled to make money. In 2024, the company announced it would cease operations. Its robots—which depended on external servers that the company could no longer pay for—would descend into a deep slumber. 

Videos of bereft children who seemed to have become deeply attached to the blue bot began to circulate online. “I don’t want her to leave,” wailed one child in a TikTok video. Desperate parents posted on TikTok, Instagram, and Reddit looking for solutions. “My autistic child is devastated and I’m pissed,” wrote one parent. “Hope Embodied gives us a couple days to say goodbye,” wrote another.
